videos.desc: Adobe stock has been a disaster, and now the CFO is selling $500,000 worth of stock. Is this another negative signal? Now, the CFO actually bought stock back in March, which obviously hasn’t worked out very well. And you normally hate to see an insider flip from buying to selling. However, in this case, the CFO is simply exercising restricted stock units and performance stock units that were granted as part of their compensation package. These units automatically converted into shares, so this wasn’t really a discretionary sale. A lot of insiders sell all of these shares immediately because they owe taxes, and selling also helps them diversify. Many executives basically treat these shares as part of their salary rather than long-term stock holdings. In this case, about 15,600 shares were converted, and the CFO had to sell roughly 8,200 shares just to cover taxes. So while the software sector—and Adobe specifically—has been struggling recently and may still not interest you, this particular sale isn’t bearish. In fact, you could even argue it’s slightly bullish, since the CFO actually held onto a portion of the shares instead of selling everything like many insiders do.

original_client_text.markup_text:
Adobe stock has been a disaster, and now the CFO is selling $500,000 worth of stock. Is this another negative signal?

Now, the CFO actually bought stock back in March, which obviously hasn’t worked out very well. And you normally hate to see an insider flip from buying to selling.

However, in this case, the CFO is simply exercising restricted stock units and performance stock units that were granted as part of their compensation package.

These units automatically converted into shares, so this wasn’t really a discretionary sale.

A lot of insiders sell all of these shares immediately because they owe taxes, and selling also helps them diversify. Many executives basically treat these shares as part of their salary rather than long-term stock holdings.

In this case, about 15,600 shares were converted, and the CFO had to sell roughly 8,200 shares just to cover taxes.

So while the software sector—and Adobe specifically—has been struggling recently and may still not interest you, this particular sale isn’t bearish.

In fact, you could even argue it’s slightly bullish, since the CFO actually held onto a portion of the shares instead of selling everything like many insiders do.
